utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. It is ominous that the witness is not here. Mr. Saxon, there's something that you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I hope it's not too ominous, Your Honour; it's simply a procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: (redacted) who, as Your Honours know, is obviously a very important witness in this case, and that evidence is obviously relevant to the credibility of that witness. Your Honour, there have been discussions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's being suggested that we may need a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, you're absolutely right. It's my lapse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not right, a more alert Judge than me is right. I'm afraid we need a redaction, and to be in closed session for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We would have a short application to make, but we're mindful of the time as well. We're wondering whether it may be the best use of time if we were to try to finish the witness first perhaps, and then to make the application later. And while the witness is coming, I would simply bring to your attention the fact that we have also disclosed the provisions which we understand to be relevant to the evidence of (redacted). We would simply indicate that those are the provisions which we, the Defence, understand to be relevant, since Ms. Residovic has indicated we have been unable to communicate with (redacted) because of her travel. We will communicate with (redacted) to verify whether those are, indeed, the provisions which are relevant to her testimony when she arrives in Skopje, and I'm being told that we are not yet in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are now in open session. The blind may be put up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honours, to redact the name of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think that witness is the subject of any protection order, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to closed session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Galeva. My name is Dan Saxon. I'm a attorney. I'm originally from the city of Boston in the United States, and I respect the Office of the Prosecutor in this case. I have some questions for you. First of all, you started working for the Ministry of Interior in April of 2002, is that right, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially as of the 1st of April, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And prior to that, you worked as a lawyer for a private company, and, as well as, you also had your own law office in the town of Strumica. That's right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the period from 1996 to 1998, when the law office was opened, up until 2002, when I went to the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Strumica is a town in the south-eastern corner of Macedonia relatively close to the borders of Bulgaria and Greece?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what kind of cases did you handle in your private law practice in Strumica?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly civil cases and economic cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to formally beginning your work in the Ministry of Interior in April of 2002, had you ever worked as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? What is the period you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to your employment in the Ministry of Interior, prior to the start of your employment, had you ever worked as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until my official employment of 1st of April, 2002, from the period from closing my law firm, I carried out -- I came to Skopje to the ministry on occasion, in view of the fact that as of the end of December, 2001, the procedure began for my employment. This was a formal procedure for approval and securing financial means for that workplace. This is why my official beginning started when the financial resources were secured in April of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. That's very clear. I'm sorry, perhaps my question wasn't clear. I'll ask it another way. Prior to even beginning your contacts with the Ministry of Interior in December 2001, had you ever worked as a police officer at any point in your life?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Had you ever worked as some sort of a crime inspector?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Had you ever received any specialised forensic training?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period of time, no; the period prior to my coming to Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Had you ever been trained as a prosecutor prior to the time you came to Skopje?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no specific training, but the exam which was a condition for opening a law firm which was at the same time a condition to work as a judge, and a prosecutor was in -- was in that context relevant, but there was no particular training.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, similarly, up until the time you came to Skopje, you had not received any particular training as an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No special training, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about your apprenticeship in the Ministry of Interior. It's my understanding you worked as an apprentice in the sector for Interpol for about two months, in April and May 2002. That's right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as an apprentice in the Interpol sector, you were given an introduction to different jobs and areas of work in that sector?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, for example, you learned about the process of issuing warrants on persons; you learned about the procedures for examining the origin of cars that were imported in Macedonia from abroad; as well as some other areas of work of the Interpol sector. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But -- and then later on, a bit later on, in mid-April, you also accepted the proposal of Spasen Sofevski, the head of the crime police department, to follow the exhumation procedures in Ljuboten. Have I got that straight?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first call was made by the head of the criminal police, Spasen Sofevski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that after that first conversation with Mr. Sofevski that you -- you had several conversations with Mr. Uslinkovski from the sector for forensics at that time, because around that time the exhumations in Ljuboten village were going on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But just so that we understand you, did you ever personally observe the exhumations as they occurred in Ljuboten? Did you go to the cemetery and observe the work?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was never personally present there. This was following the process of exhumation, which meant conversations, not going to the place of exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And after the exhumations, there were certain autopsies carried out in the Forensic Institute. Did you personally observe any of these autopsies?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And then, on the 1st of June, 2002, you took up the position of state advisor within the cabinet of the minister. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that was quite a large promotion from the position of apprentice, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The status apprentice was a phase I had to go through, because this is a formal procedure. It is regulated by legal and internal acts of the ministry. But in view of my previous work experience, this was the condition for obtaining that particular work position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, would it be fair to say that during your two months of work as an apprentice in the sector for Interpol, you made a very favourable impression on your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably this is so. If it had been differently, surely the -- there would not have been an evaluation or proposal for direct superiors in this sector and the unit which was part of the sector where I was to be called to do work in addition to the one I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sure during that time you demonstrated then strong professional qualities during your apprenticeship?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume this is so. This is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You demonstrated that you were a diligent and dedicated professional?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what my superiors said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That you're organised and meticulous?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You're good at making and keeping records?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, of course, you needed all these skills and qualities previously to run your own successful law practice in Strumica, right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Moving on to a different topic, you mentioned, yesterday, you explained that after the elections in Autumn of 2002, a new Minister of the Interior came in. That was Mr. Hari Kostov, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And he, Mr. Kostov, replaced Ljube Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday, you explained that with the coming of a new minister -- or of that new minister, Mr. Kostov, many transfers were made in the Ministry of Interior and many employees were deployed to different positions. And you also testified that other colleagues like Goran Mitevski, who had been the head of the public security bureau, left the ministry altogether. And you explained that at that point you left your position as state advisor in the minister's cabinet on the 1st of November, 2002, and you took annual leave then for several months. Have I got that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With the coming of the new government, there was a -- there were many transfers, many employees were redeployed. This was also with the director for the -- the bureau for public security, Mr. Mitevski. He voluntarily left the ministry. I was allowed to stay for a while, for a new workplace to be found for me, with the explanation and excuse that an adequate workplace for me has not been found yet; and, therefore, it would be well advised that I wait for a while or take a holiday and that I would be called in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, at that time, in November of 2002, and even before that time, when a new minister entered office in Macedonia, that new minister tended to prefer to fill posts in the ministry, if possible, with members of his own political party or other trusted political colleagues. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I can be concrete about talking about this period, with the coming of the new minister, the office of the minister was completely changed. Also, decisions were issued about numerous redeployment of workers from their current to other work positions. However, it is not to be excluded that some people remain because of their professional qualifications but surely not at that moment, after a certain period of time; and once this mistake, if I'm allowed to say, is seen and was then remedied. But it was after a certain period of time and not at that given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's fine. I understand that. But the underlying reason for these many transfers and deployments, isn't it, is that the new minister tends to prefer to fill his or her important positions with persons who belong to his or her own political party. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most frequently and most often, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was Hari Kostov's political party? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Social Democratic Unit of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ljube Boskoski, at that time, he was a member of VRMO-DPMNE. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mention that you were allowed to stay for a while. Were you also a member of VRMO-DPMNE?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On 1st of November, 2002 - I already mentioned this - I was told to leave the office and to wait a certain period of time until I was called in again and until an adequate work position was found for me where I could be deployed. On a number of occasions, I did this by myself. I made an attempt to meet with these people, I wrote to them; and, at the end of March, 2003, I succeeded in having such a meeting. It was with the then state secretary in the ministry and the director for public security. I was given a new contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Mrs. Galeva, that one of the reasons why you were selected to be a state advisor to the minister in 2002 was because you were also a member of -- of his political party. Do you think that played a role in the minister's decision?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it had a role but not the decisive role. This was not the decisive issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can, can we return to the events of April 2002. Yesterday, you described a meeting that you had with the director for public security, Goran Mitevski, and Minister Boskoski in late April 2002. And you explained that at that meeting you and Mr. Mitevski and Mr. Boskoski discussed your work to date regarding the Ljuboten case. Do you recall that testimony that you gave yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you explained to the Trial Chamber that at that meeting, Minister Boskoski told you that he wanted you to become fully engaged on the Ljuboten case and take a new work position in the office of the minister. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, eventually, a woman named Katica Jovanovska, who was an analyst working in the sector for analysis and research in the Ministry of Interior, was called into that meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Ms. Jovanovska, you understood at that time, had been compiling information about the events in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those information were primarily of an analytical nature because she used to work as an analyst in the sector for analysis and research within the ministry, and she was in charge in collecting all those analytical information that were produced within that sector. And she was charged to produce a comprehensive information that would deal with the Ljuboten case exclusively, but she failed to complete that task. She started with it, but there was no ending to the task, until she left the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you have just explained that. So Ms. Jovanovska left the Ministry of Interior, took up her new post as a judge, without providing you with the final version of the information and analysis that she had compiled?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Regarding the information, well, I did receive some notes and other working materials. I'm now speaking specifically about the information. She was tasked with producing that, and I had not received that information, while I had received some notes and other materials continuously, all up to the day when she left the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you spoke with Ms. Jovanovska's superior in the sector for analytics and research, the woman named Vasilka, Ms. Vasilka explained to you that Ms. Jovanovska had not handed over this final version of the information prior to leaving the Ministry of Interior. That's right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, effectively then, you were unable to acquire that final information?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made efforts; however, nobody knew where that information was, and it was not included in the handing over of cases, which means that there was never a finalisation to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, did you call Katica Jovanovska in her new workplace as a judge and ask her for these materials?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after she left, I asked her what happens in the future, whether she left anything that she had intended to give to me. She said that she simply left. "I gave you everything I had," she said, "and if there's something else, my colleagues from the same sector will continue working on it. If there's anything, they will continue forwarding materials to you." And I also thought that this information would be comprised by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So Ms. Jovanovska declined to give you any additional information or any final version. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the final version; otherwise, the information -- I had seen the initial version of it, but that was a text written on computer heavily edited in handwriting. There were many corrections on the initial text, and it was an information that was finished halfway. I had seen it. I had an insight into it, but I had not received the final version; although, I, of course, received other information other than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you think Mrs. Jovanovska is responsible for losing the final version?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak about it. I don't know whether she had lost it or what is the reason why she failed to hand it over or complete it. She herself would be the best witness to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you suggesting at all that Ms. Jovanovska took some material with her when she left the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it, but I haven't seen anything of the sort, so I could not make such assertions with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You say you heard about it. What did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically about that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: About the possibility that Ms. Jovanovska took some of these materials with her when she left the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you already, I had just heard rumours regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: She did not admit anything of the sort. There were no reliable assertions about this. These were only rumours that certain files were missing, certain documents were missing, and that there was a guess that that information was among those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us who told those rumours to you, or whom?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those rumours were heard. I can't say precisely names of persons. I have heard it from several persons. My only official interview was with Vasilka who was one of the heads of the sector for analysis and research, and I asked her to provide me some information or some data related to that document and the preparation. And I told you also what was the answer that I received from her. All the rest were rumours that were in circulation among the colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, of course, you're aware that the woman known as Vasilka, one of the heads of the analytical sector, you're aware that she passed away last year, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned, moving a little bit further in time, you mention that several days after your initial meeting with Minister Boskoski, you met with Director Goran Mitevski "because he was tasked with giving" a copy of all the materials that his investigative committee had gathered to you. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that the record is clear, it was Minister Boskoski who had tasked Mr. Mitevski to give you a copy of all the materials collected by Mr. Mitevski's 2001 committee. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move to a new topic, the scope of your job with respect to the Ljuboten case. Yesterday, my colleague, Ms. Residovic, asked you to explain what was your principle task with respect to the Ljuboten case. And you explained that your job was to - and I'm going to break it down into two bites - first of all, collect the comprehensive material, which the Ministry of Interior had pertaining to the Ljuboten case without going into detailed analysis or preparing any kinds of reports; and then, secondly, you said strictly collection of material in one place, that is, to place these materials that you collected in a chronological order in one place, and then to hand these materials to the directors of public security, the sector for counter-intelligence, and to Minister Boskoski. Have I paraphrased your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, I'd like to ask you if you can help us understand, please. What did you understand at that time by the term "Ljuboten case"? What was the Ljuboten case?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the Ljuboten case previously only through the media, because I came to work in the Ministry of Interior much later, after the end of that case. So the only thing I could learn was what the media offered. Once I was invited for the conversation with the head of the crime police in the MOI, and he presented his thinking and at the same time the proposal that I would tackle monitoring this case. He elaborated broadly on the case and, of course, the exhumation was going on, so that every day that event was present in the media and in the TV details about the case. Actually, only that the procedure was going on without presenting any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, let me perhaps ask a more specific question. By the "Ljuboten case," did you understand that to mean the events inside the village of Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the fact that certain persons died inside the village of Ljuboten on 12 August 2001. Was that, for you, the Ljuboten case?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically, that it was an event where some individuals have lost their lives. That was all of the initial information until I started collecting the materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And during the course of your work, during that spring and summer of 2002, did your understanding of what the phrase "the Ljuboten case" meant, did that change at all?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew before was a lot less. I had very meager information before that. Of course, when I started collecting the materials, I arrived at numerous information, numerous acts; and when I studied them, when I collected them, of course I learned much more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But is it true to say that the work that you did during that summer of 2002, it focussed on the events inside Ljuboten from 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So then your work did not include, for example, gathering information about the treatment of persons who had been detained at check-points near Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bulk of the material -- materials I gathered, of course, contained other information, other acts. But I will emphasise again, they pertained exclusively to event. Of course, there were materials dealing with a broader period of time, but, still, the purpose, the intention was to arrive at that event. So they started within a time-period before the 12th of August, but only with the intention to arrive at the 12th, to see what were the preparatory activities, what took place before that, and what finally took place on that critical date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, just so that our record is clear, when you use the phrase "that event," you're referring to the event or events that took place inside the village of Ljuboten on the 12th of August. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about an "event" since that was the notion, the term used, the event. And this is why I'm using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understand that, but I'm just trying to be clear that the definition that I gave you accurately describes what you mean by that event. That's all. I'm sorry. I don't think we could hear your response.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you use the phrase "that event," you are simply referring to what happened in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So your work, in 2002, did not include gathering information about the treatment of persons, for example, in police stations around the Skopje area, persons who had been detained in or near the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will say, again, I worked on that event only, but in the materials that I received, that I gathered, a period before and after the event was comprised as well. So there were some other material there as well, apart from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Just to simplify the matter a bit. Your task, if I understand it, was to collect materials or information that the Ministry of Interior already had in some form and put it in one place, one location, in chronological order. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And a large part of your work about the Ljuboten event involved having discussions with persons who you described yesterday as persons in leading positions who might be able to answer questions related to the Ljuboten event. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document, if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we have some binders with some documents that might make it easier for the parties to follow along, if they could be distributed, and we have a copy for the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, if you could please turn to tab number 2 in that binder, you'll see there's some numbers with gray tabs. And if you could turn to tab number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Exhibit P73. It is the decision to establish a commission to consider the circumstances and analyse the activities undertaken by the security forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to repel the armed attacks by terrorist groups on the 12th of August, 2001 in the village of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you with me, Mrs. Galeva?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you'll see this is a decision dated 13th of August, 2001. I think you're familiar with it, and signed by then Minister Boskoski. And further down in the page, paragraph 2, it says that the commission has the task to review the circumstances and analyse the activities undertaken by the security forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to repel the armed attacks of terrorist groups on 12 August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten-Skopje. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn to what is tab 3, Mrs. Galeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit P378.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Galeva, you'll see, when you get to the Macedonian version, that this is the report of the commission that Minister Boskoski had established on the 13th of August, 2001. The report is dated 4 September 2001. And we see on the first page, again, the subject is, "An examination of the circumstances and an analysis of the activities undertaken by the security forces for the Ministry of Interior to repulse armed attacks by terrorist groups on 12 August 2001." Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could take a look, please, at what is, in the English version, the last paragraph of page 1. I believe it is it on page two of the Macedonian version, Mrs. Galeva. If you turn to page 2, you'll see a paragraph starting with: "In order to carry out ..." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that paragraph reads: "In order to carry out an inclusive analysis of all aspects of the circumstances in which the events took place, as well as an expert evaluation of the manner in which the activities that particular day were implemented, a comprehensive review of the chronology of the events was carried out with a professional review of the regulative stability of this type of activity, on the basis of which the Commission affirms the following." Have you followed me in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It would be fair to say, wouldn't it, that, really, your task in 2002 and the task of the 2001 committee headed by Goran Mitevski were actually quite similar, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Similar. However, my task was to gather materials, and his task was to analyse the gathered materials. There is a difference here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, would it be fair to say that before you can analyse materials, you have to gather them first? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. You need to gather them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then, of course, when you gather them, you'd want to review the chronology of the events, right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn, please, to the bottom of page 4 in the English version; and, Mrs. Galeva, this will be the bottom of page 5 in the Macedonian version, please. If you see at the bottom of page 5, you see auto paragraph with the word "opinion" over it, do you see that, one page back? Do you see a paragraph at the bottom, and it has the word "opinion" over it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then maybe I can ask the usher assistance to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I can show the usher this. Mr. Usher, I think I could show you. It's here. We are still on tab 3, the report of the 2001 commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The first paragraph of this opinion reads the following: "The activities which were carried out by the security forces of the Ministry of Interior to repulse the armed attacks of the terrorist groups on 12 August 2001, in the village of Ljuboten-Skopje, were well-founded, justified, and properly undertaken, yet there is evidently a slight tolerable degree of individual overstepping of the boundaries of the prescribed powers, carried out by a small number of members of the Ministry of Interior, who actively participated in the event." Were you able to follow with me?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, you had received a copy of this report from Goran Mitevski when you began your work on the Ljuboten event. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you spoke with the persons in leading positions from the Ministry of Interior who might be able to answer questions about the Ljuboten event, did you ask any of them to give you a list of the names of the members of the Ministry of Interior who participated in the events in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I requested that. However, there was no such list, despite the fact that the information produced by the commission noted this, and there were some conjectures that the MOI members had participated in the event. However, despite the efforts to obtain data on any such persons, such data was not received. So it was never ascertained, it was never proven that specific persons had participated on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, but this report, signed by three very high-ranking members of the Ministry of Interior, referred to a small number of members of the Ministry of Interior who overstepped, if we can say, the boundaries of their powers on the 12th of August in Ljuboten. How could such an opinion be written without knowing who those persons are and what they did?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very many accusations, speculations in the public that was ever present in the media. It was rumoured that the members of the MOI of the police forces had participated in that event and that they perpetrated that overstepping of boundaries of power. And for that reason, when preparing the information, the committee had included such paragraph. However, all the way until the end, nothing of that was proven, nothing was ascertained. Such efforts were constantly made to find the participants in order to hold them responsible, if that was needed; but despite the huge efforts on the part of the crime police department, on the part of the sector for internal affairs under the command of which they were under the competence of which they were, still no names were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if I understand your evidence correctly, then this opinion, at least in part, is based on rumours. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this is not a question that can be asked of the witness because she did not prepare this report. We can ask her what she later could find out. But the basis on which the commission prepared the report, we had here witness Galevski and these were questions that could be put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked the witness how or whether she had tried to find the members of the Ministry of Interior who were described in general terms in the opinion of this report. And the witness -- and I asked the witness, well, without speaking to such persons or identifying them, how could this opinion be written, and the witness responded, well, there were rumours about this participation. So I think my -- I think my question, then, is a correct follow-up question. I want to know if the witness believes that rumours, the use of rumours then played an effect in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question, Mrs. Galeva. Is it your evidence that this report of the 2001 committee headed by Goran Mitevski was based partly on rumours?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in view of the fact that nothing is proved and there were many accusations about the participation of security forces in this event, there was no time to prove all this, and it was inevitable that this information need to be prepared. This is the reason why this clause was introduced, that it was possible to exist. Therefore, this is a conditional phrase. It exists as a possibility, which means that it leaves room for further investigation and proof that this is indeed what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I want to read you a part of this paragraph, again, Mrs. Galeva. It says this: "Yet there is evidently a slight tolerable degree of individual overstepping of the boundaries of the prescribed powers carried out by a small number of members of the Ministry of Interior who actively participated in the event." Tell us, please, where do you see a conditional phrase in what I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there were rumours. It was being said that members of security forces had taken part in this event. We must not forget the fact that there were security forces check-points there and in a -- and understand conditions of intensive armed attacks by members of the National Liberation Army. If there have been a direct attack of those check-points, reaction would say have been necessary. This is what leaves room to be further investigated which was impossible due to time restrictions. It was impossible to establish all of this in such a limited time-frame, so that with certainty one can claim whether something happened or not. This is -- I believe that this is a phrase based on this, what might or might not have happened. I do not exclude -- it does not exclude the possibility of either one or the other happening; however, this is a given statement without confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm very carefully listening to the questions of my learned colleague and the answers, and I think there is a misunderstanding between them. I'm looking at the Macedonian text and the English translation, because the word in the Macedonian text is what the witness is talking about. In the English, it is the one which my learned colleague is talking about. I would ask, if possible, to read in the Macedonian this segment in particular, so that the interpreters can interpret it because the report states -- it was: "The occurrence of presence was note," while the translation says: "It is evident that something is established," while the Macedonian version says to the contrary. Perhaps the witness can now read this text in the Macedonian language, so that the interpreters can interpret it directly, because this is something completely different whether something is recorded or made -- or made evident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems that there is a possibility of some difference in Ms. Residovic's view between what is in the Macedonian text and the English translation. I take it it's in the opinion. Perhaps the witness might be read the Macedonian text, and we can follow the interpretation that comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, could you please read the first paragraph of the opinion in your language, please.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The activities undertaken on behalf of the security forces of the Ministry of Interior for repelling the armed attacks of terrorist groups on day 12 August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten-Skopje are based, justified, and rightly undertaken whereby the presence of tolerant level -- negligible tolerable level of individuals swaying from the borders of regulated authorisations had been noted, carried out by a small number of members of the Ministry of Interior which actively took part in the event and case."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the difference to which you were drawing attention, Ms. Residovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these words "whereby the occurrence is noted." These are now translated "as noted." While the English translation of the text, it reads: [In English] "There is evidently a slight ..." [Interpretation] I do not know whether this has been checked or not by what the witness is explaining to the Prosecutor, or is the Prosecutor said that this is evident. If something is evident, the presumption of the Prosecution is, and this is something he always reiterate, is that this is being established. This is where the misunderstanding is occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Residovic. I'm trying to grasp the point you were making. You identified the particular passage. I think we must leave it to Mr. Saxon and the witness to pursue that if they choose or if Mr. Saxon chooses to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would simply like -- in the English translation that we have of the document, the word "is" is used. And that is, in the Prosecution's submission, the significant point here. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, did you speak with Goran Mitevski about who these persons from the Ministry of Interior who actively participated in the Ljuboten event were?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have had discussions with Mr. Goran Mitevski. However, he told me that, as of the first moment, it is being taken into account and an investigation is being made as to who these persons were who -- and this was done by the operative services, the intelligence services who were in charge of carrying this out and doing this. Mostly information was being sought by -- from Mr. Petre Stojanovski, head and assistant of crime police in the sector for internal affairs of the city of Skopje, and through OVR, unit of internal affairs, Cair. Also, information were requested from the sector of internal control at the ministry, where in any event in the case of such deviation or overstepping, a report had to be made against a concrete person so as to enable the procedure, necessary procedure to be taken, which can be led in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, would it be fair to summarize your last response by saying that Mr. Mitevski was not able to provide you with the names of the members of the Ministry of Interior who participated in the Ljuboten event? He did not have those names.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you think if you had spoke to the members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs who were present in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001 those individuals would have been able to clarify whether the persons who died at Ljuboten were civilians or not?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask you to repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you had the opportunity to speak with the members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs who took part in the Ljuboten event on the 12th of August, 2001, those persons would have been able to clarify whether the persons who died at Ljuboten were civilians. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this regard, I had exclusively and for the most part contacts with the forensics unit at the ministry because this body was exclusively in charge to follow this process; and, of course, the best information could be obtained from there. Throughout there whole period of time, I was in contact with them, I had meetings with them; and, of course, I gathered some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, that's all fine but I need you to answer the question that I asked you. I asked you a very different question. If you had the opportunity to speak with the members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs who participated in the Ljuboten event, do you think those persons would have been able to clarify the circumstances in which people died at Ljuboten, or whether they were civilians or not?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had discussions with many persons who, at that time, were in senior positions at the ministry; in particular, I will go back to Mr. Petre Stojanovski, with whom I spoke at length, because, as the first person of crime police in the internal affairs unit at the city of Skopje, he was in the best position to provide me with information about this. From what he was able to learn, true facts about persons who took part in this event could not be established. Major efforts were put in to establish who these persons might be. This was done through the unit of internal affairs, Cair, through police stations, persons who went at the site, but it was not possible to get accurate information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, didn't the 2001 commission that was led by Goran Mitevski compile the same materials that were tasked to compile?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission was set up immediately after the event. It was set up by a decision of the minister of the 13th of August, 2001. It was tasked to collect everything that pertained to that event with a chronological overview line given that should have been part of this information to be submitted to the minister. It was tasked to gather material in support of the information that was to be prepared for the minister, but it was not only this commission. There were other commissions, working groups, that dealt with this case also and including the commission which I was a part of, and we were all tasked with our own tasks to gather material that can assist in giving answers to some issues which, at that time, created major dilemmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to come back to that. But part of the materials that you put in chronological order for review by the minister in the summer of 2002 were the same materials that had been collected by the 2001 commission. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One part, yes; but not all of it. Only a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. A moment ago you told us that the 2001 commission was not the only commission, and you said "there were other commissions, working groups that dealt with this case also, including the commission which I was a part of." Can you tell us, please, what were these other commissions and working groups that addressed the Ljuboten event?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the commission which I already mentioned set up with the decision of the minister immediately after the event. It was presided by Mr. Goran Mitevski; then a commission on war crimes chaired by Mr. Apostol Stojanovski that worked on basis of complaint by injured parties; then the commission on accusations made by the Albanians as to their attitude of police forces towards them. There was unofficial working group without a decision that included Katica Jovanovska prior to my coming, and there was Jordan Arsov, a former judge, as an outside associate. So there were many such commissions, working groups. In addition, there were concrete tasks, concrete authorisations to gather material. It was not left strictly to these commissions to deal with these issues. Rather, a large group of people was engaged that should also deal with this case, so as to gather material that could be of significance of establishing the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm conscious of the time. Would this be the appropriate moment to take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. We will have the first break now and resume at five past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, before we took the break, in your last response, you mentioned that there was what you referred to as an unofficial working group without a decision that included Katica Jovanovska that was working on the Ljuboten event. Then you mentioned there was a former judge as an outside associate." Can you help us understand, please, what was this unofficial working group that included Ms. Jovanovska and who created this unofficial working group and what was it tasked to do?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the commissions that were involved, working with the decision of the minister, there were also other working groups that were working without a written decision about their tasks. They were simply told by their direct superiors that they should deal with this matter. Specifically, Mrs. Katica Jovanovska, in view of the fact that she was then working as an analyst at the sector of analysis and research at the MOI, was tasked to obtain, follow, and put in one file all materials that pertained to the conflict as a whole and, in particular, to the case of Ljuboten. There was also the outside associate for legal associate as an advisor for legal issues, Jordan Arsov, an outside associate, a former judge. He also followed these events and gave guidelines; as well as Pavle Manov [phoen], also an outside associate, that also worked on this issue. But I believe on the Ljuboten case, it was more Katica Jovanovska and Jordan Arsov that worked on this matter until I came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who directed this outside legal advisor, Jordan Arsov, to work on the Ljuboten case.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was certainly decided at a collegium of the minister and that was the decision of the advisors to the minister, that such person should be retained to work around this case. But he had some other tasks as well, and those were run in parallel. This was one of the tasks, one of the duties, and it concerned only following the information that came to the sector of analysis and research. And I believe that the aim was that he and Katica Jovanovska would gather the information, discuss them, and then organise them in a binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so, if I understand you, the advisors of Minister Boskoski, the members of his collegium, they recommended to the minister that Mr. Jordan Arsov perform this task, provide this assistance?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stress, again, his assistance was to follow all the analytical information together with Mrs. Katica Jovanovska; otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, I'm sorry. Maybe you didn't understand my question. My question was very simple. It's your evidence, then, that the advisors of Minister Boskoski, the members of his collegium, recommended to the minister that Mr. Jordan Arsov provide some assistance on the Ljuboten matter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And, then, was it Minister Boskoski who then arranged to have Mr. Arsov provide his particular assistance?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present during the event, when he was invited, the time and place when he was invited by the minister. And whether that was a one-on-one meeting with the minister or whether that was on a collegium that took place regularly in the minister's office, the minister and his advisors would participate. Certainly, he was invited during that time, and this task was given to him, among other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where would we find any report written by Mr. Arsov with respect to the work that he did?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no written report, as there is no written report from the work of Mrs. Jovanovska. I'm saying again: that was a task force or a working group that dealt exclusively with analytical information, gathering of all analytical information pertaining to this period that was compiled at the sector for analysis and research within the ministry. Part of those information were then handed over to me; and, of course, they were included in the materials that was later given to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can move on to another topic, please. Mrs. Galeva, I'd like to turn your mind, please, to the subject of the sector of the Ministry of Interior for counter-intelligence. The abbreviation that you used yesterday, UBK. Yesterday, during your testimony, you explained that the -- that the main aspects of the UBK -- excuse me, the main aspects of the work of the UBK, are, among others, to follow persons, to obtain information, and to intercept telephone conversations. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To do that kind of work normally requires a lot of people and resources, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it will also require a lot of skill and professional experience on the part of the members of the UBK who are doing that work. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If the members of the -- if the UBK, the sector for counter-intelligence, needed to identify police officers who participated in an operation, the members of the UBK could find that information, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is one of the ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to another topic, because you mentioned yesterday that after you began your work collecting materials regarding the Ljuboten event, you -- you explained that on many such occasions you spoke with Minister Boskoski about the progress of your work. Am I correct in assuming you're talking about discussions that took place during the summer of 2002; June, July, August?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. After I started working on that, after I received the decision to be deployed in the cabinet of the minister, certainly the minister was interested to learn what stage has the procedure reached and what have I managed to find. And we had discussions or those were questions asked at collegiums before a broader audience or also during informal one-on-one decisions, if the minister considered that appropriate. So he would be informed about the state of the matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there was a lot of speculation about the Ljuboten events in the media at the time, particularly after the exhumation, and Minister Boskoski wanted to get to the truth as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You need to make it a verbal response; I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There were many speculations in the public related to the Ljuboten event. There were allegations that that was an armed attack where members of the security forces of the Ministry of Interior took part; that the outcome of that was, among other things, a murder of civilians; and that those were speculations present in the public. To an overly large extent, there were criticisms coming from Human Rights Watch. There were recommendations to the government. So the minister demonstrated really significant interest to investigate and examine all this over the briefest time possible, and this is why such efforts were made to establish committees, to establish official and unofficial groups, to gather all available materials that the services in the ministries had, in order to provide many answers related to the event, to see what was actually taking place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's clear. Just to simplify this, a lot of the speculation in the media took place in the months after the exhumations and the autopsies were carried out in the spring of 2002.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were speculations always.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But those were the same speculations that were present before the start of the actual procedure, as well as afterwards, since no results were present to the public from the post-mortem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then, the exhumations and the autopsies that were performed in April 2002 did not really clarify the facts about what had happened in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001, did they?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no final report. I'm saying, in the Ministry of Interior, there was no final report; otherwise, there was a final report on the part of the Forensics Medicine Institute that was communicated to our justice system bodies; and after that, it was communicated to the ICTY. I spoke at that time with the head of the forensics police in the MOI. That was the only service that participated in that process, and I gathered some information from them, also some findings from the professor from the director of the Forensic Institute, Dr. Aleksej Duma. And from the discussions with them, many interesting conclusions were drawn. Otherwise, the expertise itself, the expert report on the materials gathered, was brought to an independent institute, independent laboratory that is located here in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva --

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us which -- in which of the reports of the Forensic Institute for which of the exhumations or autopsies we would find these many interesting conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, in your last response, you said from your discussions with people, such as the head of the Forensic Institute, Dr. Duma, many interesting conclusions were drawn. And I just wanted to ask you, if you can tell us specifically, in which of the reports of the Forensic Institute we would find these "many interesting conclusions," or the conclusions that you found interesting?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this question is unfounded in -- from the answer of the witness, because as far as can I see, in line 20 of page 40, the witness says that there were discussions with them, many interesting conclusions were drawn. And the question was from what materials, so I think that this should be the direction that my learned colleague should take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure, Ms. Residovic, that the witness will be very well able to make it clear, if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, do you want me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the question, but I think that I had already answer it previously. So, I'm stressing once again: I did not read that from any report. What I'm saying is on the basis of the discussions that I had with the head of the forensics police, Mr. Uslinkovski; and the director of the Forensic Medicine Institute, Aleksej Duma; and some time later, also with are the investigating judge who was chairing the entire procedure, Mr. Dragan Nikolovski. So it is only on the basis of discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I understood your evidence from yesterday, Minister Boskoski encouraged you to work quickly, to do as much as you could and as fast as you could. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that's because Mr. Boskoski wanted to know the truth.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you informed him, during your discussions, about how had you spoken with, what had you done, and Mr. Boskoski gave you his full support?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was always kept informed. He wanted to be informed how far the procedure has gone. He wanted to know about all things that were taking place, what contacts I had, what materials I was gathering. So he had a special interest in that, and he stressed always that it should be finalised as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, given Mr. Boskoski's special interest, when appropriate, he also gave you instructions to speak with particular heads of sectors or units who might be able to give you an answer about particular issues. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe that was mentioned during some discussions, but I primarily relied on the discussions with the other senior officers and I was already knowledgeable about issues. So I knew myself whom among the senior officers I could address and who could provide answers to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I just want to read to you a bit of a response that you gave yesterday to my colleague, Ms. Residovic, in response to one of her questions about your discussions with Minister Boskoski. This is on page 8704 of the transcript. You said: "As for special instructions, he," that's Minister Boskoski, "he let me know that a certain head of a sector of a unit could also give an answer to certain issues. So he gave me a kind of instructions, sort of to direct my activities, so I would not sway too much in this matter." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told you that he had mentioned something of the sort during the discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Minister Boskoski ever instruct you to speak with a man named Johan Tarculovski?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Minister Boskoski ever instruct you to speak with a man who owned a security company called Kometa?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: A man named Zoran Jovanovski who had the nickname Bucuk. Did the minister of suggest that you speak with that man?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Jovanovski was then in the police department when I came to work for the Ministry of Interior, if he is the person that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mrs. Galeva, and it is a very easier confusion. I'm talking about a man with the same name, the exact same name, because both that -- both those names are common in Macedonia. But the man who -- the man with the name Zoran Jovanovski, his nickname was Bucuk. He ran a security company known as Kometa. Did Minister Boskoski ever suggest that you speak with that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Minister Boskoski ever suggest that you speak with a man known as Kunta?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Two brothers with the last name Janevski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski is on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know that but I was waiting for you to finish your line of questioning. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this manner of examining the witness. I believe that it would be fair to first ask the witness whether she knows those individuals, and then to start asking such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Apostolski, but I think that this is it a matter that can be left with Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question, Mrs. Galeva. Did Minister Boskoski ever instruct you to speak with a man known as Kunta?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about two brothers with the last name Janev or Janevski?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday - turning to another topic now - you provided some testimony about the report that the organisation Human Rights Watch issued about the Ljuboten event. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss the Human Rights Watch report with Minister Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the same date when I was first invited to the minister's office, to the office of Mr. Ljube Boskoski, and let's not go back to the entire conversation. On that same date, Katica Jovanovska was invited, because she was tasked with giving the materials that she had already gathered to me. Among the other materials, the analytical information that I had mentioned already, was also the report of Human Rights Watch; and then we had some brief discussions and brief comments around this report, or maybe later during other meetings that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall what comments, if any, Minister Boskoski gave regarding the Human Rights Watch report?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I just can't say precisely whether it was on the same date or during one of the subsequent meetings, yes. And when commenting on this report, he said that it was full of unfounded, uncorroborated matters; and, of course, anyone could allege anything before the public. Anything could be put on paper. But having in mind our legal system and the presumption of innocence, until you prove that something was perpetrated, until you prove the responsibility and culpability on the part of the accused person, there is no accusation. The person is free, and they were really unfounded and uncorroborated allegations. This is why he was greatly interested in denying all the allegations contained in the report and prove the opposite. This is why he was in such a hurry to resolve the entire case as soon as possible and to resolve all dilemmas, to provide many answers to the questions raised within that. Since in the materials that I gathered later, there were a lot of contradictions, huge discrepancies within certain details of specific data.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You have explained that yesterday. Thank you. Mrs. Galeva, if you could please turn to what is tab 4 in the binder in front of you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit P355. It should be in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Galeva, I hope you a Macedonian translation of this document. It's a news report from the BBC dated the 27th of August, 2001, and the headline is: Macedonia's interior minister rejects human rights accusations." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the article begins where Minister Boskoski is denying claims that were apparently put in a new report by Human Rights Watch related to the events in Ljuboten. And sort of in the middle of the page, we see a sentence that says: "I vigorously reject the accusations." Do you see that, Mrs. Galeva?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there the Minister is quoted. First, he said there were no grounds for the claims, just above that. Then he is quoted as saying: "I vigorously reject the accusations against the interior ministry and against the regular and the reserve police forces, which have demonstrated unprecedented courage in defending Macedonia's sovereignty and territorial integrity in the past six months." Are you following with me?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then he says: "I view the accusations issued by Human Rights Watch as a classic act of framing the interior minister." And then below that, we see a sentence that says: "He," and that would be Mr. Boskoski, "said his purpose was to defend the Macedonian people's national interests and that he no intention to justify his actions." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then in the last line, Minister Boskoski is quoted from the radio as saying: "If there exists any evidence, I am prepared to account for it; although, all this is out of the question." Have you been following with me?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Wasn't one of the interests of Minister Boskoski in collecting information about the Ljuboten event was to protect what he perceived to be the Macedonian people's national interest?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please ask the question again? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sure. Well, you've explained that Minister Boskoski had a special interest in collecting all information within the ministry related to the Ljuboten event and that Minister Boskoski was anxious to get to the truth as soon as possible. Wasn't one of the motives of Minister Boskoski to put, as he is quoted here, "to defend the national interest of the Macedonian people"?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in this matter, would it be fair to say that within the minister's cabinet, at least by 2002, there was a perception that the report of Human Rights Watch was damaging to the national interest of the Macedonian people; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was such atmosphere that such comments were really annoying and tasteless. Since they were unfounded and uncorroborated, of course they hurt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The comments made by Human Rights Watch?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it was also an objective of Ljube Boskoski to protect the reputation of the Macedonian police, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In fact, it was one of Minister Boskoski's objectives to protect the reputation of the entire Ministry of Interior, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, still, the possibility was not precluded. If there were issues that go against the reputation of the police in general, as a whole, of course he would react. Of course, as the leader of that ministry, he found the reputation important. But if something was done to jeopardise that, he would certainly react.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, for example, one of Minister Boskoski's reaction was to set up a commission on the 13th of August, 2001, to investigate the Ljuboten event, right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to tab 6 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Exhibit P356.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I see do you not have a Macedonian translation. I will read a portion of this article to you. It's from the New York Times, from September 2001, and the headline says: "Report says Macedonians killed civilians in revenge." It describes the report of Human Rights Watch that was to be issued on the same day as this article appeared in this newspaper, and it refers to some of the details and allegations contained in the Human Rights Watch report. It refers to several comments that Minister Boskoski made in reaction to the Human Rights Watch report. And, at one point, about halfway down the page, on the right hand column, the article says: "He," that is Mr. Boskoski, "he also attacked Human Rights Watch which investigated the incident, calling it 'an international mercenary organisation.'" Mrs. Galeva, did you ever hear Minister Boskoski use that term in reference to Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my presence, in the presence of other colleagues on all of our joint meetings and collegia, a statement of this kind I have not heard. As I said, I heard that there were many contradictory sentences within, many statements, accusations which are unsustainable and uncorroborated.
