This was his comment for the most part regarding their report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You're somewhat familiar with Human Rights Watch because part of your task was to review their report and ascertain whether the allegations were correct. Do you believe that Human Rights Watch is an international mercenary organisation?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not like to give my personal opinion on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm asking for it.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I'm able to see so far and my experience in preparing this material, primarily I was able to read really some who horrific things which really sounded quite incredible to me. With time, by gathering all of the material, by obtaining altogether different information from that contained in this report, I gathered that there is a very large gap, which led me to a position to think that they are providing this information. The reasons for this and why they are doing this or not, they are best to judge. It is not mine to judge. I know that there was great differences and some unsubstantiated and uncorroborated matters within.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mrs. Galeva. In the English transcript, you're quoted as saying: "I gathered that there is a very large gap, which led me to a position to think that they are providing this information." But I think --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Misinformation or disinformation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. What did Ljube Boskoski say to you about this Tribunal and its investigation into the events in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In regards to The Hague Tribunal, from the very start, he was interested to be -- gather the material as quickly as possible that would be of use to the Tribunal. This is a Tribunal that should reach the last decision. We are on the other side. We are the ministry that should make available all material available and at its disposal from all professional services in the ministry. That will be for the benefit for reaching this decision, in order to establish a true, factual situation, supported by arguments and facts that will corroborate this. This is why he requested in all of these procedures that -- or procedures that went in our country at that time to include representatives from The Hague Tribunal. I can be specific, especially in the process of exhumation which was one of the most important ones. There was insistence that this not be left only to our services, that it involve the active participation of supervisors from The Hague Tribunal in Skopje in order to avoid any possible manipulation in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said Minister Boskoski said he wanted to gather the material as quickly as possible that would be of use to this Tribunal. So that was in the spring and summer of 2002, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Because, at that time, the Prosecutor of this Tribunal had asserted her primacy over the Ljuboten case. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a different topic now. You mentioned in your testimony yesterday that you had a number of meetings and/or even telephone discussions with persons who might be able to provide you with information related to the Ljuboten event; for example, you mentioned the man, the head of the crime technique sector of the police, Mr. Uslinkovski, and that had you several meetings with him. Do you recall your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, as you described yesterday, Mr. Uslinkovski gave you information related to the persons who were exhumed at Ljuboten and then who subsequently were subjected to an autopsy, right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And those discussion -- that discussion or those discussions with Mr. Uslinkovski must have been important discussions, isn't that right, with respect to your work?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you explained -- if I understood your testimony from yesterday, you explained that Mr. Uslinkovski -- that the discussions with Mr. Uslinkovski led you to meet with Professor Duma, the head of the Forensic Institute. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You -- you had several meetings with Professor Duma, and you explained that Professor Duma confirmed what Mr. Uslinkovski had told you. That's right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, again, those would have been important meetings with respect to the work that you were doing.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And your conversations with Professor Duma led you to speak with the investigating judge at the time, Mr. Dragan Nikolovski, right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And from Judge Nikolovski, you received similar information to the information that was provided to you by Mr. Uslinkovski and Professor Duma, right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so, again, those discussions with professor -- I'm sorry, your discussion with Judge Nikolovski also would have been an important meeting for your work.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You also telephoned Mr. Ljube Krstevski but he declined to assist you, right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That must have been a disappointment to you, but obviously it was a significant conversation for you because you remember it very well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where did you record the information that you received in these important discussions with Mr. Uslinkovski, Professor Duma, Judge Nikolovski, and Ljube Krstevski? Where can we find the record of these discussions?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no minutes because most often these were person-to-person meetings, and it was customary not to take minutes on the collegia. All I can say, for myself personally, on each meeting, I took personal notes, text for all issues that were raised and for all answers that I received with each of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where can we find your personal notes of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were personal notes that I took at the time. I remember at the end, when I handed over the material to the public prosecutor general, once the whole material was gathered, all of these notes were contained and were part of this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And these were materials that were eventually destined to be sent to this Tribunal. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what the public prosecutor general told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, if members of this Tribunal were to review the material that was provided to this Tribunal by the government of Macedonia in 2002, surely they will find your personal notes of these important discussions, right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be; although, there are also other evidence to this -- to this extent. What I remember surely is remembered by the other persons with whom I had conversations with, and they can confirm this in their statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That may be, but I'm asking you about your notes or whatever records you may have created. You mentioned earlier today that one of your professional strengths was the ability to make and keep good records. Why is it that you didn't make minutes of these very important conversations that you had?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Ministry of Interior, for meetings held, minutes are held exclusively by the analysts. This is not something that I can do or anyone else in a different work position. All my notes from all the conversations I had were, for the most part, talking points from these meetings, the most important points, questions or answers. These were not official minutes. This is not something that was under my competence to do. This was done exclusively by analysts at the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You became a lawyer, and you graduated as a lawyer, was it 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you suggesting that, with all of your experience by 2002, you were unable to create minutes of the -- or some other record of the conversations that you had?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, misleading of the witness. The witness said that it was not her task, not that she was not in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, please, Mrs. Galeva?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already emphasised, in the ministry, the task for taking minutes is assigned to a person employed as analyst. All other records, of course, can be led by anyone else within the framework of the work they carried out; but these were not obligatory, nor were they official records.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, when you went to speak to these important individuals, Professor Duma, Judge Nikolovski, Mr. Uslinkovski, you didn't bring an analyst with you, did you?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, then, the only person from the side of the Ministry of Interior who could have created a record of these conversations, could have physically created a record, was you, right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just to understand you, you had been given what was for Minister Boskoski a very important task, wasn't it, to get to the truth about the Ljuboten event?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in your prior law practice, your work as an apprentice, wouldn't you always try to keep full and accurate records of any aspect of your important tasks?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I had some records; but I will emphasise, once again, in this specific case, it was not obligatory to lead official reports because this was not an official commission, rather, a working group, with tasks and obligation assigned by authorisation of the minister. If it had been a commission or another working body, then, surely, there would have to have been some written records or written acts, results which would have been the result of the activities of this commission or working group. However, since this is something altogether different - I'm clarifying now - such records were not mandatory. Whether I kept my own records or not, that was really my personal business, a matter of my 3 personal belief, without anyone tasking me or authorising me to do this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You say that this was not an official commission, but you had been tasked by the Minister of the Interior to clarify or try to clarify the truth about an important event in which people had died. Are you saying this was not official part of the duties -- or part of the official duties of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a working group, yes. Official in the sense that it was not made official in a -- with a written document. In a way, the minister had the authorisation to do this in written and in oral form. In view of the fact that the situation was really critical and it was expected to achieve the final results as soon as possible that will disclose the truth, these working groups, several working groups and commissions were formed. A lot of other employees of the MOI were engaged that dealt with the Ljuboten case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that I'm sure that I understand you, are you making a distinction within the work of the Ministry of Interior between the -- the work of a working group and the work of an official commission? Does the work of an official commission have some higher level of authority or formality than the work of a working group?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a matter of procedure. The commission is set up with a decision in written form; while working group, as I clarified, can be set up with the oral authorisation. Their competencies and their importance are on equal footing. There is no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, with respect to the working group that you were participating in, in 2002, there was no reason why minutes of important meetings that were part of the work of that working group could not have been created, right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Judge Nikolovski told you that "the law provided that the investigating judge not provide information in writing to the Ministry of Interior." Do you recall that part of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what law makes that prohibition? Where can we find that law?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know this. This is not a matter in my scope of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another topic now, please. You mentioned yesterday that, at one point during your work, you telephoned Ljube Krstevski and attempted to initiate contact with him, and you testified yesterday that Mr. Krstevski refused to cooperate with you. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we assume that you reported Mr. Krstevski's response to Minister Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was Minister Boskoski's response to that information?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly only, I informed the minister, Mr. Ljube Boskoski, that Mr. Ljube Krstevski, despite my efforts to have a meeting with him, refused that proposal and that he had a very brief excuse, saying that what he knew about the event and all the written materials that he had, he had already communicated and that he could not say more than that. And, of course, I communicated this to Mr. Ljube Boskoski. What happened further, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, I'd like you to ask [sic] the question that I asked you -- excuse me, we're all tired. I'd like to you answer the question that I asked you. My question was: What was Minister Boskoski's response to this information that you gave him about your communication with Ljube Krstevski?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply, he was surprised with the answer that I communicated to him, and he told me to not take any initiative in this respect and to leave it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you aware of any other measures or actions that Mr. Boskoski took after that, with respect to obtaining the cooperation of Mr. Krstevski?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware only that the head of the criminal police force the city of Skopje regularly, on a daily basis, communicated with Mr. Ljube Krstevski. Whether the initiative for that came from the minister or not, I'm really not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ask Mr. Boskoski to order Mr. Krstevski to cooperate with you?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Any reason why not?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He already gave me the answer, that everything that was needed would be undertaken by him, that I should not take any further initiative, to leave it to him. And I expected that he would tell me anything if he needed -- if he considered it needed. Because he never told me anything, I didn't take any further action.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But when you continued not to receive any response from Mr. Krstevski, did you bring up the matter again with Minister Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not raise that issue ever again with Mr. -- but then I had regular contacts with the assistant for criminal police, Mr. Lube Stojanovski, who was on a daily basis in communication with the head of the department for internal affairs, Ljube Krstevski. So this is how I received a large number of information from him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters did not get the name in line 60, 1, where the witness did not raise the issue with Mr., and we could not get the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We need to clarify something in the interpretation, Mrs. Galeva. At the start of your last answer, you're quoted as saying: "I did not raise that issue ever again with Mr...." and then the interpreters didn't hear the name. I believe I heard you say "Mr. Boskoski." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With the minister, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you report to director of the public security bureau, Goran Mitevski, the fact that Ljube Krstevski had declined to cooperate with you?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately afterwards, I informed the director.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Mitevski's response?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he would confer with the minister, and they would decide what activities to take next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you didn't ask Goran Mitevski to order Mr. Krstevski to cooperate with you?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just informed him and I awaited for his response, and he told me, "Leave it to me. I will confer, I will discuss the issue with the minister, and then we will see what strategy we will employ."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear back from Goran Mitevski about this matter again?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss a different topic with you, if I may. You mentioned yesterday, in your testimony, you gave the Trial Chamber some information about a man named Atulla Qaili who died shortly after the event in Ljuboten. I'm just trying to understand your evidence. Did you actually read certain written records pertaining to Mr. Atulla Qaili in the course of your work in 2002?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you report what you learned about Mr. Qaili to Minister Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if I spoke to the minister about this event. I remember that I did discussion with the director, Mr. Goran Mitevski. And I also discussed it, and he was the one who sent me to discuss it with Mr. Petre Stojanovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, so, Goran Mitevski suggested that you speak to Petre Stojanovski about the death of Atulla Qaili. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other information that he already told me orally, the director. So we first had a discussion. He provided me with some information related to the case, and then he told me that I should feel free to discuss it with Mr. Petre Stojanovski, since this was in the area cover by a police station in the OVR Cair and they were potentially able to provide me with further useful information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what else, if anything, did Goran Mitevski tell to you do to ascertain how Atulla Qaili died or why he died?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was a document, an act that the person was taken to a hospital. I believe that it was the city General Hospital; that there was presence there of a judge; and that immediately after the Ministry of Interior learned about it, they have informed the duty prosecutor about the case. After that, the prosecutor requested the ministry with an act to establish the identity of that person, and, really, that was done within the ministry, within the sector for police forensics. Such establishing of identity was carried out on the basis of papillary lines, and it was proven that this was the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that, but I don't think you actually answered my question. My question was: In addition to suggesting that you speak with Petre Stojanovski, what else, if anything, did Goran Mitevski suggest to you that you could do to learn how Mr. Qaili had died. Did Mr. Mitevski give you any other suggestions?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That request, that act was sent from the ministry to the prosecutor's office, stating that we had such a case, that we had a case of a person who died at the hospital; and, after that, the prosecutor requested to carry out an expert report to establish the identity on the basis of papillary lines. Those were the basic acts that I had in my folder, and I discussed them with the director, Goran Mitevski, and with Petre Stojanovski. I discussed those issues when the identity of the person was really ascertained. Those were, really, as far as I remember, several acts related to that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understand that. That's very clear. But those acts, request for expert report, to establish the identity on the basis of papillary line, et cetera, those acts were produced, those written documents, they were produced back in August of 2001. What I'm trying to understand is, in the spring and summer of 2002, when you spoke with Goran Mitevski about your work on the Ljuboten event and he suggested to you that you speak with Petre Stojanovski with regard to the death of Atulla Qaili; that's very clear. My question is simply: Did Goran Mitevski give you any other suggestions at that time, in 2002, as to where you might find information about the cause or the circumstances of the death of Atulla Qaili. That's all. If the answer is no, that's fine. We just need an answer.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I believe that that case, as well as other cases, was included in the procedure, and the outcome of the autopsy was awaited, whether really there was a report on that person, among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you never became familiar with a report of an autopsy that was done on Mr. -- on the body of Atulla Qaili in August of 2001. You never became familiar with that report?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever visit Skopje City Hospital and ask to see the medical records there related to persons who had been detained at Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was not necessary. I already had those materials. That was a case that took place before I came to work for the Ministry of Interior, and I believe that the materials that the ministry had available were sufficient, that there was no need after such a long time to go to the hospital and ask for any reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you aware whether the Ministry of Interior, prior to your employment, had obtained the medical records from Skopje City Hospital of persons who had been detained at Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mrs. Galeva, you provided some testimony about the autopsies of persons who had been exhumed at the cemetery in Ljuboten, and you told us that when the bodies were exhumed and then subsequently autopsied, you said: "So they were wearing black T-shirts or camouflage T-shirts." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to learn that none of the autopsy reports or examinations of clothing worn by the deceased persons indicate that an individual was wearing camouflage?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is really surprising, because I did not rely on a single source. I had many sources. It would not be possible for all the sources to differ so much. There were identical elements in the discussions that I had with those persons before I received that report, and it was impossible that I would receive such report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for the record, I'm referring to Exhibits P445 through P450, Exhibit P452, and Exhibit 1D74 and 1D77.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said you had many sources about this information that some persons were wearing camouflage clothing. Can you tell us who the sources were?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many sources, those that I had mentioned already. Those are the sector, the department for police forensics within the MOI, where a team, a numerous expert team composed of several persons. Experts, experts in their respective areas, were involved in the investigation I discussed with them. Then there was the director of the Forensic Institute, Professor Aleksej Duma; the investigating judge, Dragan Nikolovski, who was the main leader of the overall procedure of exhumation and autopsy of those persons. So if one of them told me something, all the others provided identical answers regarding all of these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So each of these persons who you just mentioned, they would confirm that some of the one or more of the persons who were exhumed from the cemetery in Ljuboten were wearing some kind of camouflage clothing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You described, yesterday, a meeting that you attended in the late summer of 2002, where members of the commission to investigate war crimes were present, do you recall that bit of your testimony, and files were discussed --

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- and documents were reviewed? Help us understand something: Couldn't Minister Boskoski have assigned the Ljuboten case to this commission that he already set up to investigate war crimes?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood, I had a single contact, a single meeting with this committee. I could give you the description. They came to my office. It was a large group. If there is a need, I will enumerate the persons present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, I need you to answer the question that I asked you. My question was: Couldn't Minister Boskoski have assigned the Ljuboten case to this commission that he already set up to investigate war crimes.

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to that committee alone, because that committee dealt with many other cases and not the Ljuboten case only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So there was a commission or a committee that dealt with the Ljuboten case, among others. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, this committee was dealing with war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There was -- there was this committee for investigating war crimes, and that committee dealt with the Ljuboten case, among others, right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that committee was composed of a group of qualified professionals, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So why was it necessary, then, to start yet another project and assign you the task of compiling information about the Ljuboten matter and putting it in chronological order?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at that time there were several committees, several working bodies; and, simply, there was a need to have all the materials gathered by previous committees or the existing committees and working bodies to have them entered into a single case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So part of your task was to take the materials related to the Ljuboten event that had been gathered by the commission to investigate war crimes and incorporate that material in the single case file that you were building. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the committee dealing with war crimes, as I mentioned, I had only one meeting with them. Maybe later, I would receive some materials from them in different manner, through post or something. But all the materials that they had produced on Ljuboten case, they had the task to hand is over directly to Mr. Boskoski, to the minister, not to me. They only informed me about their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, then. So does that mean that the case file that you put together in chronological order related to the Ljuboten event did not contain 100 percent of the materials available to the Ministry of Interior, because there were some materials that the members of the commission to investigate war crimes gave directly to Minister Boskoski. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can feel free to state that the materials that I gathered was 100 percent of the materials that the ministry had available and that was supposed to be communicated to the minister, Ljube Boskoski. What the other commissions and committees did, specifically the one on war crimes, was just one part of the materials that was, of course, later handed over to Mr. Ljube Boskoski, and that was actually part of what I had already gathered as a range of materials. So many things contained in their report were also contents of the materials that I had. There was absolutely no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. Would this be an appropriate time to take the second break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, yesterday, during your examination-in-chief, you explained to the Trial Chamber that "once the police turns to the basic public prosecutor's office or to the investigating judge, at the same moment, the obligation of the police..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm getting a little bit of interference but I'll start over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You were asked a question yesterday about what happens when members of the police report a crime to the public prosecutor; and at page 8747 of the transcript, you said this: "Of course, once the police turns to the basic public prosecutor's office or to the investigating judge, at the same moment, the obligation of the police on that case ceases. "Then there is a transfer of the obligations towards the judicial bodies; in this case, to the public prosecutor's office." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We need a verbal response?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you just help us, please, where in the law or the laws of Macedonia do you find support for that proposition?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you say, roughly, where in the laws of Macedonia should one look in a particular law or laws to find support for that proposition?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, this is something that could be found in the Law on Public Prosecutor or the Law on Criminal Procedure. This is my opinion, but I am not sure, perhaps in another law as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also testified regarding the transparency of the work of the Ministry of Interior with respect to the Ljuboten event, and you said on page 8726 that: "From everything that I collected, all the materials, all the interviews I conducted, I gathered the impression that the work was completely transparent; nothing was hidden." And then at the end of the same paragraph: "Nothing was hidden. Everything was transparent, absolutely." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, if you could, please, maybe with the assistance of the usher, to turn to tab 23 in your binder. Actually, before do you that, before you do that, Mrs. Galeva, before do you that, just for a minute, are you aware that in 2003 the person who succeeded Ljube Boskoski as minister of the interior, Hari Kostov, he established yet another commission to investigate the Ljuboten event? Did you become aware of that at some point?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard about this, but I have never seen, nor have I found -- nor did I found out whether such a commission did, in fact, exist or did it do any work. I was told that, with the coming of the new minister, the decision for the previous commission is no longer in effect, which means that a new commission would have to be set up. Whether this was actually done, this is not something I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let -- I'm going to show you a couple of pieces of the work of the commission that was set up by Hari Kostov in 2003. If you turn to what is tab 23 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the first document that you should see in tab 23, is -- it is not part of Exhibit P379. It still has Prosecution 65 ter number 285.24, because this was one of the documents that, pursuant to your decision of 7 December of last year, was not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Galeva, this is a report on a meeting of the 2003 commission that investigated the events in Ljuboten. It's dated the 6th of May, 2003, and if you could turn, please, to page 2 in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For those following in English, it's the bottom of page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, if you look in the second paragraph of page 2 in your language, you'll see a paragraph beginning with: "Johan Tarculovski." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says: "Johan Tarculovski played the main role in the combat operations in Ljuboten village, and he said that while he was an escort inspector with the security sector, the previous minister, Ljube Boskoski, called him personally and gave him a verbal order to solve the case, informing him that the suspect, Xhavid Hasani, was located in Ljuboten village." And then it says: "Tarculovski and the rest of the reservists were issued weapons, semi-automatic rifles and pistols, at the CO KOB at the order of the then minister, for which there are documents on the issue and return of the items." Then there are some more paragraphs that talk about the events that occurred in the village of Ljuboten on the 12th of August. Have you been following with me?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question for you is: In your discussions with Minister Boskoski in the summer of 2002, did he mention any of this information to you?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness answered this previously. To a similar question, the witness answered that the minister never mentioned Johan Tarculovski. Again, the witness is being asked the same question. Even before I objected to this, the witness had answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is going further than simply a name. This is going to information. Please carry on, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn, please, to the next document in tab 3 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this should be Exhibit P379.02 -- I apologise, it is --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. There is no answer of the witness prior to the previous question put to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In response to the previous question, Your Honours, the witness answered "No."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that that answer has not been recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague and I agree on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next document in tab 23 is admitted Exhibit P379.01. It has ERN N000-8922, and I would just like -- this was an Official Note written by Johan Tarculovski in May of 2003. Mrs. Galeva, I can actually see that you're not looking at the document that you need to be looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I have the usher's assistance again, please. It's the second document in tab 23. It's only two paragraphs long. Excuse me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps if the Macedonian version could be put object on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would like to ask for the assistance of the court officer. If the Macedonian could be put on e-court because the Macedonian version is apparently not in our binders. It's in Judge Thelin's binder. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can follow along with me, Mrs. Galeva, this is an Official Note provided by Johan Tarculovski to the 2003 commission. It says: "The investigation commission for Ljuboten village called me. During the interview, I was asked about the way in which the reservists were issued with weapons and about their arrival and billeting and the course of operations. "They were issued at weapons at PSOLO. The people who registered for the reserve were volunteers. Since I was a local, I knew the terrain and I headed toward Ljuboten together with the other men." Mrs. Galeva, did any of the persons what you spoke with in the Ministry of Interior about the Ljuboten event mention a group of reservists who were armed at PSOLO and then subsequently entered Ljuboten village?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Minister Boskoski ever mention to you anything about a group of reservists who were armed at PSOLO and then entered Ljuboten village after that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not speak about this. At least he did not say this in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you to turn to a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could turn, please, to what is P379.02. It should be the following document in your binders. I'm hopeful that Mrs. Galeva will have a Macedonian translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, this is a document entitled, "Minutes of a meeting of the commission for inquiry into the events and incidents in Ljuboten village." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it's dated 12 November 2003. And at the bottom of the page in your version, Mrs. Galeva, you'll see a paragraph where it says: "In reply to these questions Tarculovski first explained that he had been called to the first meeting as an employee of the ministry although he was now a civilian, having given notice to the Ministry of Interior. He said that he had gone to Ljuboten of his own accord and will, that is to say, nobody ordered him to go to Ljuboten. As for the persons who were in Ljuboten with him, Tarculovski replied that he had decided to withhold their names." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's dated 12 November 2003. At the bottom of the page in your version, Mrs. Galeva, you'll see a paragraph where it says: "In reply to these questions, Tarculovski first explained that he had been called to the first meeting as an employee of the ministry; although, he was now a civilian, having given notice to the Ministry of Interior. "He said that he had gone to Ljuboten of his own accord and will; that is to say, nobody ordered him to go to Ljuboten. As for the persons who were in Ljuboten with him, Tarculovski replied that he had decided to withhold their names." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then if you turn to the next page in your version, please, you will see: "Regarding the question on the manner in which weapons were issued ..." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "... Tarculovski replied that he had received a call from the then Minister of the Interior, who told him to collect the reserve force for guarding vital state buildings." Then later on in that paragraph: "Tarculovski explained further that the then Minister of the Interior had personally ordered him to select the men." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then in the next paragraph: "Tarculovski replies that he been in Ljuboten with a large group of men, more than 100." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so that the record is clear, did you ever speak with Johan Tarculovski as part of your work?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that I did not know Johan Tarculovski, which means that I have not had any conversations with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And in your conversations with Ljube Boskoski, did he give you any information about a group of reservists who he wanted to guard vital state buildings?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, the minister did not tell me about such a group of reservists; but I know that from the very onset of the conflict in the state, both regular and reserve forces were included as part of the security forces of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mrs. Galeva, can you turn, please, to what is tab 13 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be Rule 65 ter 1141. It's a document that the Prosecution obtained after receiving the Rule 65 ter (G) list of witnesses from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't believe we have a Macedonian translation, Mrs. Galeva, but it's a document dated January --

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes .

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's a document dated January 19th, 2002, and it's a letter from Human Rights Watch to Prime Minister Ljubco Georgievski. The purpose of the letter is to complain about what Human Rights Watch refers to as "a public campaign against the Macedonian Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, and its president Mrs. Marijana Najcevska, saying that Mrs. Najcevska and the Macedonian Helsinki Committee had become the targets of intimidation and verbal assaults by cabinet members, media outlets close to the government. But then it says this in the second paragraph: "Particularly worrying are the repeated public statements by the Minister of the Interior Ljube Boskoski, who spoke to the press and appeared on two television programmes to portray Ms. Najcevska as 'state enemy number 1.'" Then it goes on to say that such attacks have been amplified public television and TV and other government controlled media. Would it be fair to say, Mrs. Galeva, if you know, that Ljube Boskoski did not have a very high opinion of Human Rights Watch or the Macedonian Helsinki Committee for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The case which I just heard about now, I'm not aware of and I cannot comment about something I had not heard or seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to comment about this particular case. I'm asking you to comment about what you know, what discussions you had in the presence of Ljube Boskoski, during the time-period when you were working in his cabinet. My question is this: Ljube Boskoski did not have a very high opinion of Human Rights Watch, did he?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say what his opinion was. I know that there were many accusations made my Human Rights Watch and that he wanted to prove the contrary and to refute such accusations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know whether Ljube Boskoski had a negative opinion of the Macedonian Chapter of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, I'd like to put you that the work of the Ministry of Interior to allegedly clarify the Ljuboten event was really not very transparent, was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thought that my learned colleague would continue the line of questioning about the previous document, which was put before the witness. My apologies for interrupting him now on another issue. But in regards to the previous document, I wish to state that this is a Human Rights Watch document. The Prosecution called Mr. Bouckaert who testified before this Court in regards to this question, and it was perhaps necessary to ask that witness these questions. I apologise again for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, Your Honour. Never mind, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let me go back to my last question, Mrs. Galeva. I'd like to put to you the proposition that the work of the Ministry of the Interior to allegedly clarify the Ljuboten event was really not very transparent, was it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. I believe it was transparent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your work, Mrs. Galeva, was intended to protect the reputation of Ljube Boskoski and the reputation of the Ministry of Interior, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to an extent, since the minister wanted to learn what had happened, no matter the consequences. So if something had happened, if some of the allegations were true, if part of those allegations were true, he was determined to hold accountable all participants, if any participants. So his objective was not just to protect the reputation and the standing of the ministry and its members, but it was completely the opposite, to clarify and to disclose the truth. And if there was somebody who should have been held accountable and responsible, then that the issue should be resolved and that person be held accountable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is it your testimony today that Minister Boskoski was even determined to hold himself accountable for the event in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as the opposite was not proven. He actually proved by this that he had the intention that I had mentioned, to detect and to clarify everything and to prove the responsibility. So he included himself here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mrs. Galeva, your work, rather than intended to provide the truth about what happened at Ljuboten, was simply intended to collect incomplete materials that were already in the possession of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, in order to transfer them to The Hague Tribunal. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was just one part of the materials, a smaller part, while the rest of the materials were gathered after I was tasked by the minister. This is how a larger volume of materials was compiled, and there you can find many issues through which you can give answers to many questions related to the Ljuboten event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You already testified earlier today that you're aware that in May of 2002, Carla Del Ponte, then the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, asserted primacy over the Ljuboten case. Are you also aware that several months of delays ensued after May 2002, while the Macedonian authorities declined to refer jurisdiction of the Ljuboten case to this Tribunal, without a formal order of this Tribunal? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard about it, that there was some delay, but I didn't go into the details of why was it done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 5th of September, 2002, Carla Del Ponte made a formal request to this Tribunal for an order to Macedonia to defer competence over the Ljuboten case from Macedonia to The Hague Tribunal? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you aware that The Hague Tribunal issued such an order of deferral to the government of Macedonia on the 4th of October, 2002?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm referring to information contained in Exhibit 1D218. Additional information on this matter, Your Honour, can be obtained in Exhibit P391.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Galeva, it was in June or July 2002 when you had your meeting with Judge Nikolovski, and he told you that he could not provide written materials to the Ministry of Interior. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And isn't it right that all of your activities, collecting information on the Ljuboten event from May to October 2002, were related to the ongoing proceedings between The Hague Tribunal and the Macedonian government over the issue of deferring jurisdiction over the Ljuboten case?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the real objective of your work was to prepare the government of Macedonia to provide materials to The Hague Tribunal once jurisdiction had been transferred from Macedonia to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe that was the purpose, but the activities and the initiative came a lot sooner. The initiative came from the Minister of the Interior before the other events and requests arrived, immediately after the event has taken place. So there was still nothing. The minister already demanded and initiated the procedure within the ministry before the justice system bodies in our state, so that the procedure would be instigated and an answer provided; and only afterwards, the Tribunal submitted its request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. We're familiar with the report that Mr. Boskoski's first commission produced. It's also true, isn't it, Mrs. Galeva, that could you have easily produced minutes of important meetings and discussions that you had with your work, regarding your work, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me again about the minutes, and I believe I already provided an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions at this time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Ms. Residovic, do you re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you do, Mr. Apostolski, I assume you had no questions of the witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, your guess was right. I have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours, and I apologise for turning towards my colleague because, simply, I thought that it was his turn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He would have come before Mr. Saxon, and it was at that point I made my assumption when Mr. Saxon stood to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Galeva, you remember that my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, asked you about your experience in the police before you were employed performing the jobs that you described before the Chamber within the Ministry of Interior. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you answered that you never worked as a police officer before that. Do you remember that as well?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you answered that you had passed the bar exam, and I'm interested whether it is necessary for a person who has passed a bar exam, whether any additional training is needed for the person to become a judge, so even an investigating judge by that token, a prosecutor, attorney, or a Defence counsel for the most severe crimes. Is the bar exam a sufficient basis for a lawyer in the Republic of Macedonia to be able to perform all these duties?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bar exam is the only prerequisite for an individual to be able to engage there such activities, those that you have enumerated: Judge, attorney, prosecutor, legal representative, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were given the task to collect all documents information about the measures undertaken within the ministry in relation to the Ljuboten case, my learned colleague asked you several questions about the persons that you had conversations with. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you the question: Since you stated that you had conversations with Goran Mitevski, with Nikola Spasovski, Spasen Sofevski, Miroslav Uslinkovski and Petre Stojanovski on numerous occasions, tell me whether you are aware, do these persons that you have enumerated have any police experience and what is their professional standing within the ministry?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, and all the way until the present time, for as long as I'm with the ministry, of course they enjoy good standing and they are considered professionals in their respective areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, if you remember, my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, asked you whether you have been a member of a political party; and if I remember correctly, you affirmed that. You said that you were a member of the VMRO, and you stated that this fact did not play a decisive role in your employment. Tell me, please, considering the fact that previously you were an attorney, to what extent was that fact of importance or otherwise for your employment at the jobs that you were performing?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was decisive, my previously work experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague, the Prosecutor, asked you several questions related to the report that you received from Katica Jovanovska. That was the Human Rights Watch report. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you received this report, did you read it?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see -- in that report, were you able to see a description of the alleged events in and around the village, at the check-points and the -- in police stations?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such descriptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the fact that you were to collect information about the Ljuboten case, my question is: To what extent did you understand the Ljuboten case considering all circumstances that are indicated in this report?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did obtain a picture of about what had happened. This is a picture, a depiction on the one hand. Of course, I needed to get a picture on the other hand as well, in order to come to my own judgment about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, in all your efforts to arrive at the information from various bodies, did you request information about all allegations contained in this report, or did you request information just regarding certain allegations? Did you attempt to clarify everything or just some of the answers from the report?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that this is all allegations. I was particularly interested about the ones regarding the Ljuboten case, but also all other events that would have allowed me to assess the reliability of what is written.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When asked by my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, you answered what was your understanding of the attitude of Mr. Boskoski when he spoke about this report; and if I understood you correctly, both he and you identified certain gaps, contradictory statements, and inaccuracies in the report. So could you tell me, first of all, considering that in the report itself the minister was mentioned, that he was standing on a balcony, and that was in command of the action, did you hear the minister ever to say that that information was accurate or that it was absolutely inaccurate, or did he have any comments to such allegations from the report?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was of special interest to me and this why I spoke about this previously with other persons from the ministry and then with the ministry, Ljube Boskoski, because he could best describe the event to me. From that conversation, I understood that he was present for a very short period of time, after the end of this whole event, in the afternoon, that is to say, but that the purpose of his coming there was to learn what had happened and what was happening. I know that, as he told me, he was in contact with Mr. Ljube Krstevski, the head of OVR Cair, and that he gave the instructions about rescuing civilian population, because at that time, it was noted that there was massive movement of the population living there from the other villages. Due to fear and being afraid of a general conflict breaking out, these instructions were given in order to rescue the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mrs. Galeva, since the Prosecutor asked what were the forces that were present at Ljuboten, if any, did you in the discussions with the then under-secretary for police, Mr. Galevski, discuss the notion of whether some police units were at Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We talked with General Galevski, and he told me that that same day he was away from Skopje. He was travelling, I believe in Ohrid. He received a telephone call from Vlada [phoen], I don't remember who exactly, and that he was told that that there is a terrible situation, that the security situation is disrupted in and around the village of Ljuboten, and that measures need to be taken immediately in order to rescue the population. Then he activated all police units in that area to go and assist of population, the same as the goal of the minister, to rescue the population and to allow the people to return safely to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, you were interested in those issues, and you learned that after the events the police was deployed to rescue the population. Was that what you are you trying to explain now, or was it my misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: SOFIJA GALEVA-PETROVSKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm mindful of the time. I don't know whether to tender some documents now. I have an additional half an hour for my re-direct, and it is obvious that the time will not permit me to complete it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We adjourn now. We resume on Monday at 2.15, not in this courtroom. I think in Courtroom I, but check the courtroom. It will be necessary, I'm afraid, for you to continue your evidence on Monday. So it will be a stay in The Hague over the weekend. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Monday, the 4th day of February, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
